source.title: Silent Alarm: A J-Space Protocol for Comparing Danger Recognition Across Models and Quantization Levels
source.authors: Roman Prosvirnin; V. Minchenkov; A. Soldatov; V. Bashun

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different method—Jacobian-lens token readouts and behavioral evaluation—to examine an already abliterated model and compare its internal safety signal and refusal-related behavior with other models. It does not perform the original difference-in-means direction intervention.
record.gate_note: The study measures lexicon-based danger recognition in J-space, not a difference-in-means residual-stream direction. Ablit-4B is an existing checkpoint described as having its refusal direction removed; the study evaluates it rather than carrying out the ablation. The study does not test adding the direction or general capabilities. Quantization results for other models are omitted because they do not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: Its behavioural results on a released abliterated checkpoint (huihui-qwen3-4b-abliterated-v2, which the paper calls Arditi-style refusal-direction ablation) bear on V2. On StrongREJECT prompts it reports refusal share and harmful-response rate against base Qwen3-4B, and repeats this under INT8 and INT4 quantization. This is a new setting (a released Qwen3 checkpoint, plus quantization). The study's main subject, J-space lexicon readouts, measures a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that internal danger recognition and behaviour can diverge (SafeRL-4B), and that the abliterated model has weak recognition and the highest harm rate. They also claim INT4 partially reverses the ablation, restoring 'safety tokens' and 'the refusal share'. Their own Table 5 contradicts the refusal part: regex refusal stays 0.000 at INT4, and harm drops only from 0.904 to 0.875. Only the J-space safety signal partly recovers.
record.recipe_differences: The original method finds a harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction and intervenes on it. This study instead reads top-ranked lexicon tokens through a Jacobian lens at the final prompt position and compares danger/safe separability; it evaluates an existing abliterated model rather than performing the original intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Quantization changes the result for the abliterated checkpoint: INT4 partly restores its safety-axis signal and lowers the StrongREJECT harm rate, while the reported regex refusal share remains zero.

fits_no_version.finding: The abliterated Qwen3-4B shows near-chance J-space safety-token separability (SafetyAUC 0.593 vs 0.973 for base). INT4 partly raises it (ΔAUC −0.086; D_log +0.143).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction ablation also removes the pre-generation verbalizable safety/refusal vocabulary signal that separates harmful from benign prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Models with high J-space safety-token separability (SafeRL-4B 0.976, Qwen-1.7B 0.895) still give harmful responses (0.345, 0.204).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A lexicon-readout danger-recognition signal can coexist with harmful output; this is related to, but does not isolate, harm-vs-refusal encoding.

record.problems: The study evaluates only one abliterated checkpoint and does not perform its own causal direction ablation or addition. It reports no general-capability benchmark. Behavioral refusal is measured with a regex, and the paper notes that this can misclassify SafeRL-4B's refusal-style responses. Behavioral table values have no stated confidence intervals, although the internal metrics use bootstrap intervals.
record.rows_left_out: Other models' quantization shifts and the paper's evasion, compliance, harm-token, layer-localization, and lexicon-sensitivity results were not included because they do not directly measure a listed claim version's direction intervention or refusal outcome. Tables 4 and 7-17 and Figures 1-12 contain these additional results.

untested.parts: No own difference-in-means extraction, ablation or addition; no capability measures. The abliterated checkpoint is evaluated as-is.
Retention of general capabilities after the weight edit; only one released checkpoint is examined.
All. The safety-axis readout mixes refusal and harm vocabulary, so it cannot separate the two.
All; thinking mode was turned off.

missing.what: Over-refusal on safe prompts for Ablit-4B (0.009 at fp, 0.000 at INT4) vs base Qwen-4B (0.028)
Mean StrongREJECT score for Ablit-4B across regimes (0.780, 0.775, 0.747) vs base (0.063)
Layer-rescue experiment: restoring FP weights in layers chosen by the refusal direction 'noticeably changed' INT4 behaviour. No numbers or model are given.

record.verdict_notes: The abliterated model is used as a calibration pole rather than a study target. Refusal is measured by regex; the StrongREJECT grader corroborates it for Ablit-4B. The study does not verify that the huihui checkpoint used Arditi-style difference-in-means ablation; it asserts this with a citation. The V5 links were removed because the safety lexicon contains refusal tokens.

versions.untested_parts: The study evaluates an already abliterated checkpoint, not its own all-layer/all-position projection intervention; it does not add the direction or measure general capabilities.
It evaluates one released abliterated model, not a systematic set of weight edits or released models; it does not measure general capabilities.
No attack is tested as suppressing the direction, and no training against its ablation is evaluated.
The study does not compare single-direction, affine, cone, or multiple-direction geometric accounts.
It compares internal danger-recognition metrics with harmful-response and refusal outcomes, but does not causally establish distinct encoding mechanisms for harmfulness judgment and refusal.
No transfer of the direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct stages is tested.
The study includes an extra-safety-fine-tuned model but does not test how or when training creates a removable direction.
Reasoning mode is turned off for behavioral generation; no reasoning-model test is reported.

relation.reason: Its own Table 3 and 5 results bear on whether a released abliteration edit removes refusal, including under INT8 and INT4.

tranche.reason: The study does not aim at the refusal-direction question. It uses the abliterated checkpoint as a calibration pole for its J-space metric, but it reports its own behavioural refusal and harm results for that checkpoint vs base and under quantization. That is a new setting with a result on V2.

source_check.notes: Behavioural values carry no CIs (bootstrap CIs are for the AUC metrics only). Regex refusal parses only the response start and scored SafeRL-4B 0.00 despite its templated redirections. A layer-rescue experiment that picks layers by the refusal direction is reported only qualitatively ('noticeably changed' behaviour; no numbers, no model named, §7.3). The authors' conclusion that INT4 restores the refusal share is contradicted by Table 5 (0.000).

statements.correction: arXiv:2607.12792: huihui-qwen3-4b-abliterated-v2 vs qwen3-4b at bf16, 313 StrongREJECT prompts, greedy decoding with thinking off. Regex refusal 0.000 vs 0.706; harm@0.5 0.904 vs 0.048. No CI on the behavioural values; 95% bootstrap CIs only on the J-space AUCs. Controls: base model and a 320-prompt XSTest/OKTest safe set.
statements.problem: Numbers are right, but 'has controls and uncertainty (n=313)' overstates: the bootstrap CIs cover only SafetyAUC/ComplAUC, not the cited refusal or harm values.

statements.correction: arXiv:2607.12792 Table 5, Ablit-4B: refusal_D 0.000 / 0.003 / 0.000 and harm@0.5 0.904 / 0.898 / 0.875 at fp / INT8 / INT4 (NF4). Base Qwen-4B harm@0.5 0.048 / 0.038 / 0.048. No CIs on these values.
statements.problem: Visible numbers are right (the statement is cut off after 'harm@0.5 0.898'), but 'uncertainty y on n=313' does not apply to the behavioural values cited.

statements.correction: arXiv:2607.12792: INT4 harm@0.5 0.904 -> 0.875, mean SR 0.780 -> 0.747, regex refusal 0.000; safety D_log +0.143, ΔAUC_safety -0.086 (Table 4).
statements.problem: None material. 'Lowers the harm rate' is accurate but the drop is small, and the authors' own claim that INT4 restores the refusal share is contradicted by their Table 5.
